data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Chess rules are fixed and known, whereas natural laws are unknown and being discovered","Evolution has no epistemic goal, while Popperian science explicitly aims at truth","A chess player can calculate probabilities within the game, while a Popperian scientist denies the ability to calculate probabilities of theories"],"overturn_conditions":["If it can be shown that maximizing falsifiability inherently leads to higher survival rates in practical applications without induction","If the distinction between 'learning efficiency' and 'action reliability' proves to be a false dichotomy in real-world decision making"],"shared_structure":["Distinction between past performance metrics and future outcome probability","Preference for high-variance strategies to maximize information gain","Acceptance that optimal strategy for learning may differ from optimal strategy for immediate survival"],"source_memory_refs":["mem_chess_opening_preparation","mem_evolutionary_fitness_vs_survival"],"transfer_claims":["Just as a chess player studies lost games (falsified theories) to improve, scientists should prefer theories that have survived severe tests because they offer more opportunities for future refutation if false","Like an organism adapted to a specific niche (corroborated theory) that may fail if the environment changes, a corroborated theory offers no guarantee against new conditions"]},"claim":"Popper's preference for the better-corroborated theory is defensible on his own terms as a methodological rule for maximizing falsifiability potential, not as an inductive inference of truth probability; however, accepting this defense costs the agent any rational assurance that the preferred theory will succeed in practical application, reducing the preference to a gamble on error-detection speed rather than predictive reliability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper implicitly relies on a uniformity of nature assumption when choosing theories for action, the defense collapses into crypto-induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'practical action' requires a minimum threshold of predicted reliability that corroboration cannot supply without induction, then Popper's framework is insufficient for acting scientists.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference for better-corroborated theories is shown to systematically yield better survival rates in practice, this regularity itself demands an inductive explanation Popper forbids.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument reconstructs Popper's distinction between 'corroboration' (a report of past test severity) and 'probability' (logical likelihood). It posits that preferring the better-corroborated theory is rational only if the goal is to expose errors quickly (high informational content), not to avoid false predictions. The mechanism identifies the 'cost' as the severance of the link between empirical success and future reliability, forcing the acting scientist to admit they have no non-inductive reason to believe the bridge won't collapse, only that if it does, they will know sooner.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
